Tim Wilson still keen on super for housing, but won't touch 12 per cent guarantee
There's a superannuation conference going on in Melbourne, where Treasurer Jim Chalmers yesterday announced plans to change investment rules for super funds.
Today, it's Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson's turn. He doesn't like Chalmers' idea, as we have already heard. But he also gives some detail about his own ideas.
The idea of letting first homebuyers access their super, he says, is still appealing. No details, but a strong declaration:
"Prioritising income in retirement over home ownership... lacks economic and human logic," he says. "We do not want to be a nation of retired renters."
But he is also clear he will not touch the 12 per cent compulsory super guarantee, which One Nation wants to let some people access.
"That's a 'full stop, that's it' kind of commitment," he says, accusing One Nation of treating super "flippantly".
Chalmers has already reacted to the speech, accusing Wilson of wanting to "swing a wrecking ball through superannuation and make Australians poorer in retirement".
Unemployment rate jumps to 4.9 per cent
The unemployment rate for October has risen sharply to 4.9 per cent, from 4.7 per cent in September, seasonally adjusted.
Roughly 43,500 jobs were shed in the month while the participation rate fell by 0.2 of a per cent.
The Reserve Bank has stated that an unemployment rate between 4.5 per cent and 5 per cent would be needed to bring inflation back down to its target range of between 2 and 3 per cent.
Take a look at the ABC's business blog in the link below for more details on that story.
Government broadly looking at civil preparedness, Marles says
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says the federal government is looking at civil defence preparedness.
The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence is taking submissions and examining Australia's civil preparedness.
The UK government has launched a campaign urging residents to be ready for an emergency and have at least three days worth of supplies.
Marles says while we face challenging strategic circumstances, the government isn't issuing those type of edicts out to the Australian people.

"We are looking at civil defence preparedness more broadly. That's an issue which has been raised firstly in the Defence Strategic Review but in both the National Defence Strategy 24 and 26," Marles says.
And that's where we'll leave that press conference with Richard Marles.
Australia remains steadfast in support for Ukraine despite APEC photo: Marles
The acting prime minister says Australia remains steadfast in support of Ukraine, despite Anthony Albanese appearing in a banquet photo with the Russian president at APEC in China.
Albanese stood in the back row next to the Canadian prime minister. Vladimir Putin was standing front and centre alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.
Richard Marles says the prime minister was obliged to pay respect to the host country and participate in the photo.

"When you go to these meetings, you pay respect to the host country, you participate in the family photo. That's what has happened here. We've done that. Our prime minister has done that, along with other world leaders who are in exactly the same position as Australia," Marles says."That photo does not for a moment change our position in respect of the war in Ukraine."

"When you go to these meetings, you pay respect to the host country, you participate in the family photo. That's what has happened here. We've done that. Our prime minister has done that, along with other world leaders who are in exactly the same position as Australia," Marles says.
"That photo does not for a moment change our position in respect of the war in Ukraine."
Coalition fails to suspend standing orders in the Senate
Jumping out of that press conference for a moment. I've been keeping an eye on that suspension of standing orders motion in the Senate while the acting PM speaks.
It seems Labor has teamed up with the Greens to vote down the motion moved by Liberal frontbencher Jane Hume.
The Coalition's motion called on the federal government to establish a Senate inquiry into corruption in the construction industry.
Let's go back to Richard Marles's press conference in Nowra.
Marles urges Coalition, crossbench to back gas reservation scheme
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has urged the Coalition to back Labor's domestic gas reservation scheme.
Labor's reservation scheme would require Australian gas producers to set aside at least 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market.
Marles has told journalists a gas reservation scheme will place downward pressure on gas prices.

"The Coalition and the other parties in the Senate have a really important decision to make in terms of considering the government's gas reservation legislation in the parliament right now, and that is whether or not they're going to support Australian manufacturing and Australian jobs," Marles says.
"What we are doing by putting in place a gas reservation is increasing domestic gas supply which will help put downward pressure on gas prices."
Acting PM again defends sale of defence sites
Richard Marles has once again defended the government's backflip on the sale of the four historic defence sites.
The federal government has promised to keep four of the 67 defence sites that were earmarked for sale earlier this year.
Victoria Barracks in Sydney, Victoria Barracks Melbourne, Fort Queenscliff and Point Cook (RAAF Williams), will be spared sale and instead transferred from Defence to the finance department.

Yesterday, the Coalition, Greens and crossbench teamed up in the Senate and passed a motion condemning the government for moving Defence personnel out of the barracks, and calling on it to reverse course.
The acting prime minister says he needs to sometimes make difficult decisions to build the capability of the defence force.

"We have been operating many facilities which are underused, in some cases not used at all. That's why we undertook the defence of state audit back in 2023," Marles says."We simply can't afford to be spending hundreds of millions of dollars maintaining bases that we don't use. We need that money to be investing in capabilities such as what you see behind me."
"We have been operating many facilities which are underused, in some cases not used at all. That's why we undertook the defence of state audit back in 2023," Marles says.
"We simply can't afford to be spending hundreds of millions of dollars maintaining bases that we don't use. We need that money to be investing in capabilities such as what you see behind me."
Marles announces expansion of navy's maritime combat fleet
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles is holding a press conference from HMAS Albatross at Nowra on the NSW South Coast.
Marles is announcing an expansion of the navy's maritime combat fleet with the addition of two MH-60R Seahawk helicopters.
The acting prime minister says the helicopters will increase the Navy's ability to conduct anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare.
Marles says Australia must have a highly capable navy, and that helicopters paired with frigates greatly enhances that capability.

"They have a range of sonar capabilities which enable the best ability to detect submarines. They have other surveillance capabilities on them which enable them to do greater surveillance activities," Marles says.
"When we think about the kind of defence force that we need to meet that strategic moment, the navy is central to that. Navy aviation is an is a critical element of that."
Coalition moves to suspend standing orders on construction corruption
Liberal frontbencher Jane Hume has moved to suspend standing orders in the Senate to debate corruption in the construction sector.
The motion accuses Labor of trying to "rewrite history" by saying they have taken stronger action than the Coalition against the CFMEU.
It calls on the federal government to establish a Senate inquiry into corruption in the construction industry.
"The standing orders must be suspended, they must because Australians deserve to know why this government keeps voting down an inquiry into corruption in construction," Hume says.
"Corruption in construction is so profoundly important and yet this government continues to vote down scrutiny of that corruption in construction in this parliament."
Labor frontbencher Malarndirri McCarthy says the suspension is unnecessary and that the federal government doesn't tolerate corruption.
"There is no need for a suspension president on this particular topic or any topic, you have ample opportunity at any other time of senate business to bring this forward," McCarthy says.
We're standing by to see how it goes in a vote.
McDonald says Coalition wants to see gas prices set at a 'fair level'
A move to carve out Western Australia from Labor's gas reservation scheme allays some of the Coalition concerns with the policy.
The WA premier reached an agreement with the federal government to be excluded from the scheme because that state has its own market.
Shadow Resources Minister Susan McDonald says the Coalition is still concerned the legislation is "littered" with ministerial discretion which she says doesn't give investors confidence.
McDonald says the Coalition remains concerned about the "must sell" provision and the requirement for gas producers to meet 110 per cent of supply.
Speaking to News24, the shadow minister also wants to see gas prices set at a "fair level".

"It doesn't need to be a high level. It just needs to be a fair level, a fair level that reflects the cost of production and at the moment gas is trading at about $10," McDonald says."This is probably about the best price that industry has seen for a long time. Combined that with the higher costs of doing business in Australia this is certainly getting close to what the cost of production is."
"It doesn't need to be a high level. It just needs to be a fair level, a fair level that reflects the cost of production and at the moment gas is trading at about $10," McDonald says.

"This is probably about the best price that industry has seen for a long time. Combined that with the higher costs of doing business in Australia this is certainly getting close to what the cost of production is."
Coalition calls for national framework to stamp out disruptive classroom behaviour

A national survey released earlier this year found one-third of school time is lost to student misbehaviour, and NAPLAN tests show Australian students are not meeting expectations in numeracy and literacy.
Shadow Education Minister Julian Leeser earlier this year unveiled plans to introduce lessons on "western values" to the curriculum, to restore "national pride".
He's now calling on parents and carers to support teachers to crack down on bad behaviour.
"We as parents need to take parental responsibility for our kids and need to back our teachers in creating the classrooms we need so they can teach and kids can learn," he says.
The Coalition is proposing several measures to improve behaviour, including a survey to build an evidence base, and a national framework with guidance to be rolled out across the country.

They also plan to link funding to teacher education, by potentially removing funding for universities and courses that don't follow best practice on things like phonics, explicit teaching and practical behaviour management.
Leeser acknowledges screen time has certainly contributed to bad behaviour but says there's a range of factors.
"[Devices] are disruptive and affect concentration spans," he says.
"We want to ensure we have common principals and supporting materials for schools to roll out effective behaviour management".
Shoebridge criticises PM for appearing in APEC photo with Putin
Greens leader David Shoebridge has criticised Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's decision to pose alongside the Russian president in an official APEC Summit photo.
Albanese is in China for the two-day summit and appeared in a group photo overnight with Vladimir Putin and other world leaders.
The prime minister says he's respecting the wishes of the host country to take part in the photo while making clear Australia's opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
But Shoebridge says the PM should have taken a much tougher stance.

"The prime minister should be putting tougher sanctions on Russia at the moment, stopping Russian oil coming into Australia, being purchased by Australian motorists and feeding the Russian war machine," Shoebridge says.
"Instead, he is travelling round the world getting photos with the bloke," he said on his way into Parliament this morning.
Hogan coy on whether WA gas scheme carve-out would be enough to win over Coalition
Nationals frontbencher Kevin Hogan hasn't said whether a carve-out for WA in Labor's gas reservation scheme legislation will be enough to win the Coalition's support.
Labor's gas reservation scheme would require gas producers to set aside at least 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market.
Yesterday, WA Premier Roger Cook confirmed he reached an agreement with the federal government to be excluded from the scheme because that state has its own market.
Hogan has told ABC Radio National Breakfast that the Coalition wants the scheme to ensure more domestic approvals of gas projects.

"We support the gas reservation in principle. Obviously, there's other things that we want to be part of this. We want more gas brought onto the market. Gas is an important export for us. It's important for our domestic energy needs as well," Hogan says.
ACTU welcomes mandatory safety and security guardrails for AI companies
The Australian Council of Trade Union (ACTU) secretary says the outsourcing of Australian jobs overseas "undercuts the values of Australian workers".
Qantas, Canva and Bunnings are among a growing number of Australian companies who have announced job cuts in recent weeks.
Some of those jobs have been affected by artificial intelligence and shifted overseas.
Earlier this month, the government announced mandatory security and safety guardrails for AI developers following the OpenAI hack.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Melissa Donnelly says it's disappointing to see corporations take the "easy and lazy road" to offshore jobs rather than upskill their workforce.
She has welcomed the mandatory guardrails announced by the government this month.

"We have been calling for these kinds of guardrails and clear regulatory power for some time so we're really pleased," Donnelly says."But the ongoing question is going to be whether or not workplace laws are fit for purpose in the age of AI."
"We have been calling for these kinds of guardrails and clear regulatory power for some time so we're really pleased," Donnelly says.
"But the ongoing question is going to be whether or not workplace laws are fit for purpose in the age of AI."
Nationals senator says Australian cricket team must come clean on Sandpapergate
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie has weighed in on the evolving Sandpapergate saga engulfing the Australian cricket team, saying the team must now come clean about the incident.
Last night, Cameron Bancroft, the player that was caught using sandpaper to tamper with the ball in 2018, released an explosive statement claiming the entire Australian team knew about the plot.
The allegations echo those in former batter Usman Khawaja's memoir, which thrust the incident back into the headlines earlier this month.
Yesterday, Cricket Australia announced a forum for players and staff involved in the Test match at Cape Town to discuss their recollection and perspective of the incident.
Speaking on Channel Nine this morning, McKenzie said the actions of that day had shamed Australians.
"It wasn't just the Australian cricket team that was shamed through this process, it was indeed all of us because they do represent us and they're supposed to be the best of us," she said.

"I think when you read Bancroft's words, you can't help but feel for him. They carry a lot of weight because he has nothing to gain by telling the truth because he literally has lost everything through this scandal."It was beholden on all of these men to tell the truth at the time, and they need to do so now."

"I think when you read Bancroft's words, you can't help but feel for him. They carry a lot of weight because he has nothing to gain by telling the truth because he literally has lost everything through this scandal.
"It was beholden on all of these men to tell the truth at the time, and they need to do so now."
Beef export tariffs to be a key objective of Albanese's APEC China visit, Marles says
Export tariffs on Australia beef will be a key objective of the prime minister's visit to China, Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says.
Australia reached 100 per cent of an annual beef import quota in June. In response, China imposed an additional 55 per cent tariff on Australian beef exports.
Yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese indicated he would raise beef export tariffs with Chinese officials during his visit.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Marles says removing the tariffs would benefit the trading relationship.
"This would be a benefit to China to have our beef be more available within China and that's the point that the prime minister will make," Marles says.
"Seeing this specific line of trade being advanced is a key objective here but it speaks to the broader objective which is advancing our trade with China and other countries within APEC."
Marles says he understands 'grievance' from Elton John's about artists and AI
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has responded to a plea from British star Elton John to protect artists from artificial intelligence.
In a recorded address to the ARIAs yesterday, John urged the Australian government to protect artists from artificial intelligence training their models on creatives' work.

"You have a duty to protect Australian artists and their work. Don't let AI use any Australian artists' work without full permission. Please protect the next generation of Australian artists," John said.
Speaking to News24, the acting prime minister says creatives should be "completely compensated" for their work.

"I definitely understand the sense of grievance that Elton John has that others in the creative industries have, and we want to do something about it," Marles says."You can't do anything about it by turning your back on it, by yelling at AI, by putting your head in the sand. You have to engage and that's what we are seeking to do."
"I definitely understand the sense of grievance that Elton John has that others in the creative industries have, and we want to do something about it," Marles says.
"You can't do anything about it by turning your back on it, by yelling at AI, by putting your head in the sand. You have to engage and that's what we are seeking to do."
Work starts on NDIS plan management overhaul

National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) Minister Jenny McAllister is pushing ahead with the government's planned overhaul of the scheme, which is expected to save taxpayers $1.4 billion over forward estimates.
A key part of the reforms is plan management, with the government today announcing a new Management Plan Panel to strengthen oversight and crack down on fraud.
The government says some plan managers have been claiming funding for goods and services that participants either don't need or never receive.
Between July and September this year, the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) rejected 3,600 claims worth $5.8 million due to suspected fraud, misuse of funds or non-compliance.
The new panel is designed to tighten safeguards and stop operators who do the wrong thing from overseeing taxpayer-funded spending.
Existing plan managers are being invited to help shape how the panel will work.
"Establishing a Plan Management Panel means we can build a market that operates with integrity, sets high standards and makes accountability clear," McAllister says.

📹 Elton John calls on Australian government to protect creative work from AI
British artist Elton John has called on the federal government to protect Australian creatives from artificial intelligence.
The federal government is consulting about the best way to amend copyright laws to protect artists' work amid the rise in AI.
AI models are trained on data scraped from the internet, including copyrighted materials taken without their owners' consent.
In a recorded message to the ARIA awards yesterday, the British star said the government must not let AI use artists' work without permission.
Acting PM says government remains committed to acquiring Port of Darwin
Yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese couldn't provide a timeline as to when the federal government will acquire the Port of Darwin.
Chinese-owned company Landbridge was provided a 99-year lease to the port. But Albanese promised to acquire the port before the last election.
Landbridge has launched international legal action to try to stop the acquisition, arguing it's "discriminatory" and breaks Australia's free trade agreement with Beijing.
Speaking to News24, Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles also couldn't place a timeline on the acquisition given the legal proceedings.
But he says the government remains committed to acquiring the port.

"Landbridge has walked down a different path and that gives rise to legal proceedings and they have their own timeframe and so we can't do anything about that," Marles says."But but we stand committed to seeing the Port of Darwin end up in Australian hands and we'll continue to pursue the process."
"Landbridge has walked down a different path and that gives rise to legal proceedings and they have their own timeframe and so we can't do anything about that," Marles says.
"But but we stand committed to seeing the Port of Darwin end up in Australian hands and we'll continue to pursue the process."
Marles defends PM's appearance in APEC banquet photo with Putin
Acting PM Richard Marles has defended the prime minister's decision to appear in a leaders photo with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appeared in the banquet photo with other world leaders at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.
Speaking to Channel Seven, Marles says taking part in the APEC photo is all part of the job of attending multilateral meetings.
But he says Australia's position in relation to the war in Ukraine remains unchanged.

"The family photo is a part of APEC and it's about respecting the host country, and that's what we've done and that's what other world leaders who are in that photo have done ... world leaders who take exactly the same position that we have in relation to the war in Ukraine," Marles says.
"Our position in relation to the war in Ukraine could not be clearer and our support for Ukraine could not be more steadfast."
PM expected to address APEC summit, hold talks with Mexico's president
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has a busy day ahead in Shenzhen, as world leaders gather for the main event of the APEC summit.

First up is the traditional leaders' "family photo", which will likely again see Albanese alongside some of the world's most powerful figures, including US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Albanese will then address the summit, where leaders are discussing economic cooperation and prosperity across the Asia-Pacific.
Later, Albanese is expected to meet Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum for bilateral talks, with trade and investment ties between the two countries on the agenda.
Xi Jinping gives Donald Trump a personal welcome upon arrival in China
Chinese President Xi Jinping has made a rare move to personally welcome US President Donald Trump as he touched down in Shenzhen for the APEC summit.
Xi greeted Trump at the bottom of the stairs of Air Force One, with the pair shaking hands and sharing a brief hug.
It's an extraordinary gesture from the Chinese leader, who has never personally greeted a visiting head of state at the airport since becoming president.
The welcome came complete with a red carpet, military honours and fighter jets flying overhead.
It's also a case of returning the favour, after Trump personally welcomed Xi on the tarmac in Washington in September.
But the show of warmth comes at a delicate time for relations between the world's two largest economies, with tensions over trade, tariffs and technology.

It also sets the scene for today's highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the leaders are expected to discuss some of the world's biggest geopolitical flashpoints, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Albanese appears in APEC group photo alongside Putin
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has appeared in a group photo alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in China.
Albanese is standing in the back row next to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, while Putin is front and centre alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.
The photo was taken at a leaders' banquet in Shenzhen, ahead of the summit's traditional "family photo" on Thursday.
Albanese has previously indicated he will likely take part in the official photo out of respect for China as host, despite Australia's strong opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"I will bear in mind the wishes of our host," he told reporters in Shenzhen.
But Albanese insists Australia's position on the war remains unchanged and that any peace deal must be on Ukraine's terms.

1 in 7 underpaid migrant workers took steps to recover wages, report says
A significant number of migrant workers in Australia are being underpaid, but only a small portion are trying to get their money back, partly because some are afraid they will lose their job.
That's according to a new study out today by the Migrant Justice Institute (MJI), which noted two-thirds of the almost 10,000 migrants they surveyed in 2024 were not getting paid what they should.
The MJI's study revealed only one in seven of those underpaid workers took steps to recover their unpaid wages.
Their report noted 28 per cent of workers were concerned their visa or immigration pathway would be jeopardised if they took action.
About a quarter also did not know what to do or how to access help, and almost a third feared they would lose their job if they spoke up.
The MJI's co-executive director, Laurie Berg, who co-authored the report, said speaking up can "cost a migrant worker everything".

"For migrants in Australia, underpayment has become the expected price of a job," she said."Their silence is a rational response to the system that makes speaking up too risky, too hard, and too unlikely to pay off."
"For migrants in Australia, underpayment has become the expected price of a job," she said.
"Their silence is a rational response to the system that makes speaking up too risky, too hard, and too unlikely to pay off."
Assistant Immigration Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said the MJI's report was "deeply concerning".
"It confirms what we have known for a while; that migrant workers are the most vulnerable workers in the Australian economy and subject to exploitation," he said.

"That's why our government introduced a series of measures to toughen penalties, to improve enforcement, and to provide support for migrants to report where they're not being paid properly or they're being undercut on conditions."
